note: Parametric surface responses, not textures. UC's axm-material-library carries texture entries keyed by channelHint; this pack carries the SCALAR AND LAYER behaviour those textures are modulating. Map each entry into your library as a family (values become constant channels; 'breakup' becomes a roughness/base-color texture) or feed it straight into a renderer that has these inputs. Nothing here is verified against your renderer: treat every entry as declared_contract_match_not_tested until you have looked at it.
why: Doll-like realism is almost always the same five absences: (1) light never travels INTO the surface, (2) roughness is one number everywhere, (3) there is no oriented micro-structure, (4) there is no grazing-angle response, (5) surfaces are single-layer. Each family below exists to break one of them.

axes.subsurface: How far light travels inside before leaving. Skin, wax, marble, leaves, milk. Its absence is the single biggest cause of the doll look: without it, skin is painted plastic.
axes.sheen: Retroreflective fuzz at grazing angles. Velvet, wool, peach skin, dust on cloth, fine facial vellus hair.
axes.anisotropy: Roughness with a direction. Brushed metal, hair, silk, vinyl records, turned wood.
axes.clearcoat: A second smooth layer over a rough one. Car paint, varnish, lacquered wood, wet surfaces, eyes.
axes.breakup: Micro-variation in roughness and colour that has nothing to do with the shape. The single cheapest anti-CG move.
axes.transmission: Light passing through. Glass, resin, thin leaves, ears and nostrils against a light.
axes.iridescence: Colour that changes with angle from thin-film interference. Oil, soap, beetle shells, tempered steel.
axes.layering: Wear, grime, moisture and age that sit ON a material rather than being baked into it.

families.purpose: The direct answer to doll-face. Three layers: oily top, dry epidermis, red dermis beneath.

subsurface.note: Red travels furthest. Unequal radii per channel is what reads as flesh rather than tinted wax.

sheen.note: Vellus hair. Gives the grazing-angle halo real faces have.

clearcoat.note: Sebum. Should be higher on forehead and nose, near zero on cheeks — drive it with a map.

breakup.note: Pores. Without this, roughness 0.52 everywhere is what the eye reads as plastic.

sweating.note: Wetness is a clearcoat change, not a base-colour change. Darkening the albedo instead is the classic mistake.

families.purpose: Sheen-dominant. Nothing else looks like this, and its absence makes all cloth read as painted foil.

response.note: Velvet is almost entirely edge light. A flat-lit velvet ball should be nearly black in the centre and bright at the rim.

families.purpose: The everyday surface most often rendered as plastic sheeting.

layers.note: Fibre lift at seams and elbows.

families.purpose: Anisotropy. A brushed metal without direction is just grey plastic with a highlight.

anisotropy.note: Highlight must stretch across the grain. Direction should follow the part, not the UV, or curved parts break.

families.purpose: Layered, not uniform: bare metal, oxide, grime — three different materials on one object.

response.note: Where a layer sits (edges vs cavities) is what makes an object look USED rather than dirtied uniformly.

families.purpose: Clearcoat over flake. The reference case for two-layer surfaces.

response.note: The clearcoat highlight and the flake sparkle must be at different depths. One layer cannot do this.

families.purpose: Anisotropy plus subsurface plus grain-locked breakup.

subsurface.note: Only a little — but it is why real wood glows slightly at thin edges.

families.purpose: Subsurface in a hard material — the thing that separates marble from grey plastic.

breakup.note: Veining is large-scale; pores are small-scale. You need both scales or it reads as a photograph on a ball.

absorption.note: Colour must come from absorption over thickness, not from base colour. That is why real glass edges are green and faces are clear.

families.purpose: Two-sided translucency — the reason CG foliage looks like cut plastic.

response.note: Backlit leaves must go BRIGHTER, not darker. If your renderer has no thin-wall transmission, fake it with a back-facing emissive term driven by light direction.

families.purpose: Angle-dependent colour. Cheap to add, instantly reads as 'not plastic'.
The honest version of the look everything currently has — so you can tell the difference deliberately.

breakup.note: Crazing. Even a perfect glaze is not perfectly uniform.

families.purpose: High roughness with real grazing response — not just a dark base colour.

layers.note: Tyres and grips shine where hands and roads touch them.

if_your_renderer_lacks_these.no_subsurface: Approximate with a wrapped-diffuse term (light wrapping past the terminator by ~0.3) plus a red-tinted rim. It is not correct, but it removes most of the doll signal.
if_your_renderer_lacks_these.no_sheen: Add a Fresnel-weighted term at high grazing angles with the fabric's own colour, weight ~0.2.
if_your_renderer_lacks_these.no_anisotropy: Stretch the roughness map along the grain direction. Crude, visible, still better than isotropic.
if_your_renderer_lacks_these.no_clearcoat: Render a second pass of the same geometry with low roughness and additive blending, masked where the coat is.
if_your_renderer_lacks_these.no_layers: Bake curvature and cavity maps once per asset and use them to blend two complete materials. Most of 'used' is just that blend.

how_to_check_you_have_it: A flat-lit sphere of each material should be distinguishable from every other one with the colour removed. If two look the same in greyscale, one of them is not a material, it is a tint.
Backlight every character: ears, nostrils, fingers and any leaf must brighten. If they darken, you have no transmission.
Rotate one object 360 degrees under a fixed light. If nothing about the highlight changes shape, you have no anisotropy and no iridescence anywhere in the scene.
Render a grey-only scene. If it still reads as real, your materials are doing the work. If it collapses into plastic, your colour maps were carrying the realism.
